strengths: Addresses practical and important problem of cross-domain deployment for E2E autonomous driving
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including cross-city generalization, active learning, robustness to degradations, and long-tail scenarios
Strong empirical results: 16% L2 error reduction, 54% collision rate reduction with GP trajectory prediction on VAD-T
Flexible framework compatible with different base E2E models (VAD, SparseDrive) without requiring LLMs
Effective uncertainty-guided active learning via GP predictive variance
Good visualization (Figure 2) demonstrating improved representation separability with RoCA
Detailed training procedure, pseudocode (Algorithm 1), and computational cost analysis provided for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited dataset diversity: evaluation only on nuScenes with two cities (Boston, Singapore); no validation on Waymo, KITTI, or other datasets weakens cross-domain robustness claims
Codebook construction methodology critically underspecified: clustering algorithm, hyperparameters, and sensitivity analysis all missing, yet this is a core component affecting performance
Significant computational overhead (27-36% latency increase) for real-time autonomous driving applications not thoroughly analyzed or justified

Weak theoretical justification for GP choice: why GPs are suitable for cross-domain robustness insufficiently motivated; connection between token reconstruction and trajectory prediction not rigorously established

Crucial design choices lack justification: codebook structure (Nego=48, Nagent=64, C=64) appears arbitrary; gradient freezing during basis token learning unexplained; loss term weighting strategy missing
Uncertainty calibration not addressed: no calibration error metrics, reliability diagrams, or validation that GP uncertainties are trustworthy for safety-critical applications
Claims not fully supported: 'online adaptation' mentioned in abstract but never evaluated; 'long-tail robustness' demonstrated on only three scenario types
Limited baseline comparisons: VLP comparison in appendix only, no comparison with other domain adaptation methods (adversarial adaptation, self-training, feature normalization)
Collision rate metric possibly insensitive: rates of 0.09-0.2% extremely low; missing metrics like success rate, comfort, or trajectory smoothness
No failure case analysis: which domain shifts are handled well versus problematic; when does the basis codebook become insufficient not discussed

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem of cross-domain generalization in end-to-end autonomous driving
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including cross-city transfers, robustness to image degradations, active learning, and long-tail scenarios with detailed ablations
Consistent empirical improvements across multiple metrics (L2 error, collision rate) and two different base models (VAD-T, SparseDrive-S)
Well-documented reproducibility with training procedures, hyperparameters, computational analysis, and algorithm pseudocode in appendix
Clear presentation with informative visualizations (e.g., t-SNE analysis in Figure 2 showing improved token cluster separation)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: GP-based domain adaptation is not new (references [10, 17, 20] already use GPs for this); this work primarily applies existing techniques to E2E driving, which is incremental

Critical lack of justification for core claims: the paper never explains why GP basis tokens learned from ground-truth trajectories help with domain shift—the mechanism appears circular and lacks theoretical grounding

Overclaimed probabilistic nature: claimed 'probabilistic inference' is primarily variance-weighted losses (standard practice); ego and agent trajectories are modeled independently, not as a true joint distribution despite claims
Questionable three-stage training procedure with no justification or ablation for freezing components in different stages; joint optimization might be more effective but is not explored

Modest empirical improvements with limited scope: 10-30% gains across limited domain shifts (only Boston-Singapore from same nuScenes dataset); no evaluation on other datasets (Waymo, Argoverse) or characterization of what causes domain differences
Non-trivial computational overhead not adequately addressed: 27% latency increase (59.5→75.7ms) is significant for real-time autonomous driving, but dismissed as 'slight'
Incomplete ablation studies: Table 6 shows only cumulative effects; individual loss term importance, joint vs. staged training, basis codebook size sensitivity, and kernel choice are not ablated
No statistical significance testing: results lack error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite strong claims

Limited baseline comparisons: only VAD and SparseDrive tested; no comparison with other domain adaptation methods (domain adversarial training, standard regularization); VLP comparison uses different protocol

Complex loss function with multiple weighted terms (reconstruction, trajectory, classification, triplet, KL divergence) suggesting high-dimensional hyperparameter tuning, but sensitivity analysis is absent
Open-loop evaluation only; no closed-loop simulation with actual autonomous driving stacks limits real-world applicability assessment

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical cross-domain generalization in E2E autonomous driving
Sound technical approach with principled GP formulation and clear three-stage training pipeline
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including cross-city transfer, image degradation robustness, long-tail scenarios, and active learning
Consistent improvements across multiple scenarios and two different base models (VAD-T, SparseDrive-S)
Practical contributions including uncertainty-guided active learning and unsupervised domain adaptation without ground truth labels
Strong reproducibility details with Algorithm 1, training times, computational analysis, and clear hyperparameter specification
Honest treatment of limitations and clear presentation with effective figures and motivation
weaknesses: Evaluation limited to single dataset (nuScenes); lacks validation on Waymo, KITTI, or other autonomous driving benchmarks

Insufficient justification for technical choices: RBF kernel selection not motivated, basis token codebook construction 'bijective mapping' not clearly enforced, hyperparameter values (C=64, N_code=112) not justified
Missing direct comparisons with cited domain adaptation methods (AdapTraj, Dual-TT); comparison with VLP relegated to appendix using different evaluation protocol
No statistical rigor: lacking confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing; some improvements small (0.65→0.63 m); targeted subset only 689 samples
Gaussian assumption in GP formulation not validated; high-dimensional token embeddings may cause numerical issues with kernel inversion
Active learning criterion (highest variance) not compared against alternatives; may select hard edge cases rather than representative samples
Mechanism linking variance-weighted losses to long-tail performance not rigorously established; variance correlation with trajectory difficulty in new domains unclear
Limited ablation depth: no specific variance-weighting comparison, no basis size sensitivity analysis, no analysis of GP module's cross-domain transferability
Figure 2 tSNE visualizations can be misleading regarding global structure preservation
Safety discussion limited for safety-critical autonomous driving application; failure mode analysis absent

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across closed-loop, open-loop, cross-city, image degradation, and long-tail scenarios with consistent improvements across multiple base models
Strong empirical results: 11.7% ability improvement on Bench2Drive, significant sim-to-real gains, and superior performance on long-tail events and adverse conditions
Practical plug-and-play design that works with different E2E models; no additional inference cost in source-domain training mode; supports multiple adaptation paradigms
Interpretable approach with good token space visualization showing improved clustering and well-calibrated uncertainty estimates demonstrating superiority over MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles
Good reproducibility with detailed algorithms, training procedures, hyperparameters, and timing information provided
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (GPs, token codebooks, basis learning) are well-established; applying standard GP to E2E driving is relatively incremental

Weak theoretical justification: lacks principled explanation for why joint modeling of p(e,a,trajectories) improves cross-domain generalization; connection between uncertainty and domain robustness is purely empirical

Potential circular dependency issue: base model trained to match GP predictions (Eq. 7) while GP is trained on base model tokens; training convergence and error accumulation in unsupervised adaptation not adequately addressed

Computational overhead dismissed too quickly: Table 10 shows 25-27% latency increase during inference; 37+ hours total training time is substantial; claimed 'no extra inference computation' is misleading for training regularization mode

Codebook construction under-specified: trajectory sampling and clustering procedures vague; no sensitivity analysis on codebook quality/diversity; fixed hyperparameters (Ncode=112, C=64) not justified across domains

Experimental rigor gaps: no error bars/significance tests despite multiple experiments; modest improvements in some cases (<1-2% on collision rate); limited failure case discussion; comparison with VLP only in appendix using different protocol

Incomplete technical details: positive/negative class selection for triplet loss not specified; trajectory space validity constraints not discussed; design choices lack motivation (e.g., why RBF kernel specifically)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse datasets (Bench2Drive, nuScenes, NAVSIM, DriveArena), domains (sim-to-real, cross-city), and scenarios (closed-loop, open-loop, long-tail, degradations)
Plug-and-play design demonstrating compatibility with multiple base E2E models (ORION, SSR, SparseDrive, VAD) without architectural changes
Practical contributions including unsupervised domain adaptation without ground-truth labels and uncertainty-guided active learning
Thorough ablation studies examining loss components (Table 11), kernel functions (Table 12), and codebook diversity (Table 13)
Consistent performance improvements across all evaluated scenarios with proper visualizations of learned token representations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applying well-established GP techniques (Yasarla et al. 2020b, 2021, 2022a,b) to E2E driving via basis token codebooks; core components (GP reconstruction, variance-weighted loss) are straightforward

Unclear mechanistic explanation for why GP-based token reconstruction improves cross-domain generalization; connection between token separability and domain robustness not rigorously established; missing theoretical analysis

Significant computational overhead contradicts abstract claim of 'no extra inference computation': 27% latency increase (59.5→75.7ms for VAD-Tiny) when using GP for trajectory prediction, which achieves best results

Absent statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing despite modest improvements (5-15% typical); all results appear to be single runs on modern neural networks with inherent stochasticity

Unfair adaptation comparisons: RoCA uses pseudo-labels from pre-trained GP via Eq. 7 while baseline methods adapt from scratch; isolating GP regularization contribution from pseudo-labeling advantage is unclear

Critical design choices under-explored: basis token sampling/clustering procedure not specified; extensive hyperparameter search space (Nego, Nagent, C, D, kernel) with limited ablation guidance; only one kernel bandwidth explored
Long-tail robustness claims weakly supported: Table 17 shows inconsistent improvements (Resume 35.4%, Overtake 8.3%, 3-Point Turn 6%); long-tail evaluation limited to nuScenes

Incomplete evaluation of claimed capabilities: online adaptation mentioned as contribution but not experimentally validated; active learning only evaluated on cross-city transfer with moderate improvements over MC Dropout/Ensembles (Table 8)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (Bench2Drive, nuScenes, NAVSIM, DriveArena) and domain shifts (sim-to-real, cross-city, image degradations) with rigorous closed-loop and open-loop evaluations
Plug-and-play framework demonstrating consistent improvements across diverse base models (VAD, SSR, SparseDrive, ORION), showing 11.7% mean ability gain with ORION and 27.8% with SSR
Flexible adaptation framework supporting multiple modes (source regularization, supervised/unsupervised adaptation, uncertainty-guided active learning), addressing practical deployment scenarios
Strong empirical results including sim-to-real transfer improvements (L2 from 0.98→0.68 for ORION), cross-city adaptation gains, and superior long-tail scenario performance
Clear intuitive visualization through t-SNE projections demonstrating improved token separability and semantic organization compared to baselines
Thorough ablation studies justifying design choices (loss components, kernel functions, codebook diversity, planner types)
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification for why GP-based regularization specifically improves domain generalization; connection between uncertainty weighting and cross-domain robustness is intuitive but lacks formal analysis

Non-trivial computational overhead with 26-33% latency increase (75.7ms vs 59.5ms for VAD-Tiny) and reduced inference throughput (13.2 vs 16.8 IPS), potentially limiting real-time deployment applicability despite claims of minimal inference cost

Complex three-stage training procedure (pre-train base model → learn basis tokens → finetune with regularization) lacks sufficient justification; no ablation study on whether all stages are necessary or if procedure can be simplified

Critical hyperparameter choices inadequately justified: codebook size (Ncode=112, C=64, D=256), basis trajectory sampling procedure not detailed, and choice of RBF kernel despite Table 12 showing RQ achieves better performance (0.52 vs 0.55 L2)

Insufficient analysis of basis token learning mechanisms: how Ncode·C trajectories are initially sampled is under-specified, contribution of individual basis tokens unknown, and sensitivity to initialization not explored
Missing comparisons with recent domain-invariant objectives and uncertainty quantification approaches; VLP comparison (Appendix D) uses different evaluation protocol reducing comparability
